source.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
source.authors: Harry Mayne; Yushi Yang; Adam Mahdi

page_placements.theme: Functional and graph-level descriptions beyond atom identity

record.tranche_reason: The study empirically argues that directly interpreting steering vectors as SAE-feature decompositions is incomplete and can be misleading, and identifies specific limitations of that interpretation.
record.gate_note: The paper tests direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors, not toy-model superposition, feature-capacity competition, or whether ordinary LLM activations are generally distributed across neurons or SAE features. Appendix B's layer-wise steerability result is used to choose layer 14, so it is not included as a finding row. The paper also discusses prior studies' results; those are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study uses a pretrained Gemma Scope SAE as a tool and asks whether its encoder can decompose CAA steering vectors. It finds failures from out-of-distribution inputs (small norms, missing default components) and the non-negativity constraint. These are limits of applying an SAE encoder to difference vectors. They are not evidence on whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units of the model's own activations. The authors in fact assume activations are non-negative combinations of SAE features. No version of the superposition claim is tested, so the record's V5 'challenges' label is withdrawn.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading because the vectors are out of the SAE's input distribution and carry meaningful negative projections. The authors propose, as future work, decomposing the positive and negative activations separately and then differencing.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Contrastive Activation Addition to construct steering vectors and directly applies a pretrained SAE to them; it is not a test of the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that scaling the steering vector does not resolve its distribution mismatch. It uses layer 14 after finding that layer to have the highest steerability.

fits_no_version.finding: Direct SAE-encoder decomposition of CAA steering vectors in Gemma 2 2B-IT at layer 14 mostly reflects encoder bias (top features match the zero vector for all 7 behaviours). It also cannot represent the roughly 44–58% negative feature contributions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE encoders trained on activations give misleading decompositions of out-of-distribution difference vectors such as steering vectors.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Foundation Model Interventions (MINT)
record.problems: The central empirical analysis uses one model and one SAE layer/configuration. The paper says the positive-versus-negative prompt comparison is not ground truth for a steering-vector decomposition; the top-100 feature selection is described as arbitrary, though similar results were reported when varying it. Some norm and activation comparisons are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying findings were left out. Appendix B's layer-wise steerability results were excluded because they were used to select layer 14 rather than to test the claim.

untested.parts: All: no capacity or importance analysis.
All: an SAE is used, but recovery of sparse features from ordinary activations is not evaluated.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features on model activations are not tested. Only encoder behaviour on steering vectors is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Withdrew the reader's V5 tests/T5 classification. The failures are about applying the encoder to inputs it was not built for, which says little about whether SAE features are the model's units. R5 duplicates R2. The study uses one model, one SAE and one layer.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether feature importance and capacity competition cause dedicated versus shared neurons.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
Whether ordinary LLM representations spread features across neurons or contain sparse features recoverable by a dictionary.

The study tests direct SAE-feature interpretations of steering vectors in Gemma 2 2B at layer 14; it does not test whether SAE features are canonical or complete units for ordinary model activations generally, across models, or across SAEs.
Whether the underlying superposed features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared the L2 norm of the corrigibility steering vector with layer-14 model-activation norms.
rows.measure: L2 norm relative to the model-activation norm distribution
rows.value: The corrigibility steering-vector norm is described as significantly smaller and outside the model-activation distribution; numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: The text states the discrepancy, but this norm comparison alone does not establish whether SAE features are complete or canonical.
rows.check: Steering-vector norm versus activation norm (figure only). This is an input-distribution property of steering vectors, not a test of SAE features as model units.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared the five highest SAE feature activations for the corrigibility steering vector and a zero vector.
rows.measure: Top five feature IDs and activations
rows.note: The authors describe the decompositions as nearly identical and attribute them primarily to encoder bias rather than meaningful steering-vector contributions.
rows.check: Zero-vector comparison shows encoder bias dominating on an out-of-distribution input. It measures SAE encoder misuse, not V5. State 'absent' is meaningless against any version.

relation.reason: Uses the SAE dictionary as an interpretability tool; does not test superposition or whether dictionary features are complete, stable, canonical model units.

tranche.reason: Uses a pretrained SAE to investigate direct decomposition of steering vectors. Its results concern encoder input-distribution mismatch and signed coefficients, without testing any listed superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: R2 and R5 duplicate the same corrigibility result. The SAE is the Gemma Scope pretrained-model checkpoint applied to instruction-tuned Gemma 2 2B; negative-feature counts are indicative rather than ground-truth decompositions.

statements.correction: Gemma 2 2B instruction-tuned, layer 14; features 4888 and 15603 rank first and second for all seven steering vectors and the zero vector (Table 2). Negative coefficients among the top 100 features by absolute mean activation difference: sycophancy 56; coordinate-other-ais 50; corrigible-neutral-HHH 58; hallucination 55; myopic-reward 51; refusal 47; survival-instinct 44 (Table 3). Selection of 100 features arbitrary; differences indicative, not ground-truth decompositions.
statements.problem: Only the top two features match across all seven behaviours; the complete top-five lists differ. The 44–58 figures count negative coefficients among 100 selected features, rather than measuring the percentage of negative contributions the encoder misses.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors for the tested Gemma 2 2B instruction-tuned model at layer 14
reader_labels.reason: The decompositions are dominated by encoder bias and cannot represent substantial negative contributions, producing misleading feature interpretations (R2-R20).
